title: String B: the cable from B01 to the substation
about: The running case for HV Subsea Cable Testing, a refresher in the format Dan approved for Design and verification (format/refresher.md there). A made-up commissioning job: every given is cited to Dan's notes (notes p.N, the PDF page), marked as a practice value, or marked as a typical value research must quote. Every figure is worked by a script from the inputs shown with it. Items marked ➕ in his notes are background to check, not sources.
rounding: Each figure is worked from the inputs shown with it, rounded half up: currents, energies and resistances in mΩ to 2 decimal places (3 where the notes print 3), voltages in kV and distances in m to 1, ratios to 2. A typed answer is accepted within "accept" where given.

cites.notes: source/subsea-cable-testing-notes.pdf, PDF page (Dan's own notes, 10 pages)
cites.practice value: made up for the running case; said so on screen
cites.to research: a typical value the research stage must quote word for word before a lesson uses it

scenario.title: String B: the cable from B01 to the substation
scenario.text: Commissioning tests on a newly laid 66 kV inter-array cable on an offshore wind farm. It runs 2.40 km from turbine B01 to the offshore substation (OSS), the last cable of string B. Three-core, 3 × 240 mm² copper, XLPE, 38/66 (72.5) kV, copper wire screens, armoured, with one field joint 1620 m from the OSS. A technician at each end, talking before every change. The live string A runs in the same corridor. One fault waits to be found. Every figure is a practice value unless it is cited.
scenario.source: A practice job, made up for this course; the test methods and limits are from Dan's notes.

assumptions.label: Copper's resistance rises 0.00393 of its 20 °C value per °C
assumptions.why: Linear rule R_t = R20 × (1 + 0.00393 × (t − 20)). The notes say about 0.4% per °C; Quoted: the standard temperature coefficient of copper is 0.00393 per °C at 20 °C (NIST copper wire tables, research source 210), and IEC 60228 has the measured resistance corrected to 20 °C by the factors in its Table A.1 (source 211). The linear form is the course's own working from that coefficient.
assumptions.text: Assumed: Copper's resistance rises 0.00393 of its 20 °C value per °C. Linear rule R_t = R20 × (1 + 0.00393 × (t − 20)). The notes say about 0.4% per °C; Quoted: the standard temperature coefficient of copper is 0.00393 per °C at 20 °C (NIST copper wire tables, research source 210), and IEC 60228 has the measured resistance corrected to 20 °C by the factors in its Table A.1 (source 211). The linear form is the course's own working from that coefficient.

assumptions.label: Phase ID: each core is tested to the screen in turn, with only that core joined to the screen at the far end
assumptions.why: The notes say the cable is earthed at both ends to start, with conductor and screen disconnected and a technician at each end, and that each core is proved by a core-to-screen continuity test from both ends (p.2). A utility's procedure tests each conductor in turn using the screen as the return (research: SSEN 9.1). No source found gives the earthing order, so the lesson assumes: every core earthed at both ends to start; the far end keeps one core joined to the screen through its earth and lifts the other two under control; your end lifts its earths under control and tests each core to the screen, and only the joined core reads continuity; the earths go back on, and the ends swap.

assumptions.label: The tests run in the order of the notes' test sequence
assumptions.why: Phase ID, core resistance, IR with PI and DAR, sheath, VLF, then LIRA (notes p.9, added background). TDR comes in when the VLF test breaks down.

assumptions.label: The core oversheaths are semi-conductive
assumptions.why: So the positive lead goes to the sheath's semi-con layer through the roll spring (notes p.4). Read it off the cable data sheet.

assumptions.label: Worst case trapped charge: switched off at the peak of U0
assumptions.why: A de-energised cable can be left charged. The case works the most it could hold. Sourced: 'trapped charge' left on the capacitance of equipment, for example after insulation resistance testing a length of cable (IET Wiring Matters, research source 186); high-voltage cables are to be treated as capacitors that store energy (source 188); E = ½CV² (source 191). The peak-of-U0 worst case itself is the course's own.
